title: Syllabus Types — A Field Guide

pts: Organises a course around a sequence of grammar structures, moving from simpler to more complex forms.
Its strength is systematicity — nothing is left to chance in coverage of the grammar system.
Its weakness is an ordering driven by grammatical complexity rather than by communicative need.

items: Look at the grammar column of the contents page.
List the grammar points in order.
Ask: what principle orders them (simple to complex? frequency? tradition?)
Mark any point where a later unit depends on an earlier one.
Note one advantage and one limitation of the order for your learners.
Compare two coursebooks at the same level.
Ask learners which grammar they needed but had not yet met.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A typical structural sequence at A1–A2: be → present simple → can → present continuous → past simple of be → past simple regular → past simple irregular → comparatives → going to → present perfect. Advantage: systematic coverage; clear progression for teachers and learners. Limitation: learners may need past tense to tell a story long before the syllabus reaches it.

body: Purpose: to show a structural syllabus as a sequence. Content: a staircase of ten steps, each labelled with a grammar point from be at the bottom to present perfect at the top. A small figure climbs the stairs. Style: clean, one colour. Board version: steps with labels.

items: English Grammar Profile (Cambridge, free online). Compare the textbook order with the CEFR levels at which learners typically use each structure.

blocks.x: The contents page of the class textbook.

pts: Organises around communicative functions (apologising, requesting, complaining) and notions (time, quantity, location).
Grammar still appears, but in service of the function rather than as the organising principle itself.
This syllabus type shaped the shift toward communicative language teaching from the 1970s onward.

items: Show a situation: You want to borrow a friend’s bicycle.
Ask learners what they would say. Collect several versions on the board.
Point out that the function (requesting) can be expressed in many grammatical forms.
In pairs, learners receive cards with other functions (apologizing, inviting, complaining) and write two ways to express each: one casual, one polite.
Share and build a class ‘functions’ chart.
Add notions: time, quantity, location (How long? How many? Where?).
Compare how the same function is expressed in a home language.
Support: provide a bank of phrases to sort by function.
Stretch: rank phrases from least to most polite.

lines: Requesting: Give me your bike. / Can I borrow your bike? / Could I borrow your bike, please? / Would you mind if I borrowed your bike?
Function: what we do with language (request, apologize, invite).
Notion: concepts we express (time, quantity, location, frequency).

body: Purpose: to show the functional logic. Content: a central circle labelled ‘Requesting’. Around it, speech bubbles of increasing politeness from casual to formal, arranged clockwise, each with a short phrase. Style: warm colours, clear text. Board version: circle and phrases.

items: Padlet (free plan). A board with one column per function; learners add phrases they hear in films or conversations.

blocks.x: A functions chart on chart paper, added to throughout the year.

pts: Organises around high-frequency words and the grammatical patterns they typically occur in.
Grammar emerges from studying how frequent words behave, rather than being imposed as an independent structure list.
Directly compatible with the vocabulary-frequency principles from Unit 5.

v: Twelve example sentences with the word way

items: Give learners twelve sentences containing way.
Groups sort them by pattern (the way to…, by the way, in a way, on my way).
Discuss: what does each pattern mean?
Learners write one new sentence for each pattern.
Ask: why might a course be built around common words like this?
Use another high-frequency word: get, take, thing, time.
Find the patterns in a textbook reading passage.
Support: provide the four pattern headings.
Stretch: learners find patterns using SkELL (see digital tools).

lines: Is this the way to the station? (route)
By the way, did you finish the homework? (changing topic)
In a way, he’s right. (partly)
I’m on my way. (travelling now)
There’s no way I can finish it today. (impossibility)

blocks.x: A lexical syllabus (Willis 1990) teaches these patterns because they are frequent and useful, and lets grammar emerge from them.

body: Purpose: to show lexical syllabus logic. Content: the word way in the centre of a starburst, with five rays each ending in a pattern and example. Style: bright, energetic, legible. Board version: word with rays.

items: SkELL (free). Search way to see frequent patterns in real English.

blocks.x: A page from a graded reader; learners hunt for patterns of one word.

pts: Organises around real-world tasks (booking a hotel, resolving a complaint), with language emerging from what each task demands.
Grammar and vocabulary are addressed reactively, in a post-task language focus stage, rather than pre-specified.
This syllabus type previews Tier II, where task-based learning becomes the central methodology.
points.who: Rod Ellis, "Task-Based Language Learning and Teaching"

v: A sequence of tasks on one theme

items: Choose a theme (a school fair). List real-world tasks: survey classmates, plan stalls, make posters, write invitations, present the plan.
Order tasks from simpler to more complex.
Teach one task per lesson using the task cycle (Unit 6): pre-task, task, report, language focus.
Language focus in each lesson responds to what learners needed during the task.
At the end, review what language was learned. It will not match a grammar list, and that is the point to discuss.
Use Prabhu-style reasoning tasks: timetables, maps, puzzles (Prabhu 1987).
Combine with a structural backbone: one planned grammar focus per week.
Support: provide models before each task.
Stretch: add constraints to tasks (a smaller budget, a time limit).

blocks.x: A task sequence for a school fair:

lines: Task 1: Survey five classmates on their favourite stalls. (asking questions)
Task 2: Decide on four stalls as a group. (suggesting, agreeing)
Task 3: Make a poster for one stall. (describing, persuading)
Task 4: Write an invitation to parents. (formal writing)
Task 5: Present the plan to the class. (organizing a talk)

blocks.x: A reasoning-gap task in the spirit of the Bangalore Project:

lines: Here is a train timetable. You need to reach Hubballi before 2 p.m. and you cannot leave before 7 a.m. Which trains can you take?

body: Purpose: to show a task-based syllabus. Content: five task cards in a row, each with an icon (clipboard, discussion, poster, envelope, microphone). Beneath each card, a small bubble labelled ‘language that emerged’. Style: clean, playful icons. Board version: five boxes.

items: Google Forms (free). Learners build their Task 1 survey and collect classmates’ answers.

blocks.x: Paper survey sheets and chart-paper posters.

body: In the Bangalore Project, N. S. Prabhu’s team taught English to school classes in South India through tasks such as interpreting timetables and maps, without a grammatical syllabus. Prabhu argued that grammar is acquired best when learners’ attention is on meaning (Prabhu 1987). The project influenced task-based teaching worldwide, and is one of the best-known contributions from India to international language-teaching research.

pts: Organises around the four skills as distinct strands, each with its own progression.
Common in EAP and exam-preparation contexts where each skill is assessed and reported on separately.
Risk: without deliberate integration, skills can be taught in parallel without ever combining, unlike Unit 3's integrated approach.

items: Read the specification of an exam your learners take (a state board English paper, for example).
List what each section tests: reading, writing, listening, speaking, grammar.
Build a four-strand plan: a progression for each skill across the term.
Mark at least three points where strands are deliberately integrated (Unit 3).
Check the balance against learners’ needs (Unit 2).
For EAP classes, add a fifth strand: study skills (note-taking, referencing).
Compare strands in two different exam boards.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A skills-based strand for writing across a term:

lines: Weeks 1–2: sentences and paragraphs.
Weeks 3–4: informal letter.
Weeks 5–6: formal letter or application.
Weeks 7–8: short essay.
Weeks 9–10: exam-condition practice.

blocks.x: Integration point: week 5, a reading of a formal letter provides the model for writing.

body: Purpose: to show separate skill strands with integration points. Content: four parallel coloured ropes running left to right, labelled listening, speaking, reading, writing. At three points, the ropes are tied together in a knot labelled ‘integrated task’. Style: clean, simple. Board version: four lines with three circles joining them.

items: Google Sheets (free). A term plan with one row per strand and one column per week.

blocks.x: A term plan on chart paper, one colour per strand.

pts: Most published courses blend structural, lexical and task elements rather than committing to one pure type.
Recognising the blend in a coursebook clarifies which parts to trust as systematic and which to supplement.
A mixed syllabus is not a compromise to apologise for — it is usually the most practical real-world design.

v: The class textbook; the state or board syllabus document

items: For each unit of the textbook, list what it is organized around: grammar, functions, vocabulary, tasks, skills.
Count how often each appears.
Name the blend: for example, ‘mostly structural with a skills strand’.
Decide which parts to trust as systematic and which to supplement.
Share your analysis with colleagues teaching the same book.
Compare the textbook with the official syllabus document: do they have the same logic?
Ask learners what they think the book is ‘about’.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Naming the blend for a typical school textbook:

lines: Structural backbone (a grammar point each unit) + thematic topics + reading-comprehension skills strand + occasional writing task.
Implication: speaking and listening may need supplementing; the grammar order may need adjustment when learners need a form earlier.

body: Purpose: to show a multi-strand syllabus. Content: a pie chart-like wheel divided into unequal coloured segments labelled structural, lexical, functional, task-based, skills. A second wheel beside it shows a different blend. Captions: ‘Coursebook A’ and ‘Coursebook B’. Style: clean, no exact percentages. Board version: two circles with segments.

items: Google Sheets (free). A tally table and a simple pie chart.

pts: The syllabus specifies content and sequence; the curriculum is the larger plan including aims, methodology and assessment.
Confusing the two leads to treating a syllabus document as though it answers questions about method or evaluation it was never meant to.
A scheme of work (Unit 14) sits between the two, translating syllabus content into a delivery plan.
points.who: Jack C. Richards on curriculum vs. syllabus

v: Three documents: the curriculum or policy framework, the syllabus, your scheme of work

items: Place the three documents side by side.
For each, note what questions it answers: why, what, when, how, how well.
Draw the relationship (Figure 12.7).
Identify any question none of them answers (for example, how to assess speaking).
Discuss with colleagues who is responsible for answering it.
Use NEP 2020 and NCF-SE 2023 as the curriculum layer; the state syllabus as the syllabus layer.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Curriculum: aims, values, methodology, assessment principles (why and how).
Syllabus: content and sequence (what).
Scheme of work: timing and delivery for a class (when, and in what proportion).

body: Purpose: to show nested planning documents. Content: three nested boxes. Outer box: ‘Curriculum: aims, methods, assessment’. Middle box: ‘Syllabus: content and sequence’. Inner box: ‘Scheme of work: this class, this term’. Small arrows show influence flowing inward. Style: clean, three shades. Board version: nested rectangles.

items: DIKSHA (Government of India platform, free). Access state and national curricular resources and textbooks aligned to them. [VERIFY current content for your state.]

blocks.x: Printed copies of the official syllabus kept in the staff room.

pts: Exam-driven contexts often need a structural or skills-based backbone to satisfy assessment criteria.
Communicative-priority contexts often suit functional or task-based organisation better.
The right choice is a context decision, not a universal 'best' answer — this is a toolkit, not a hierarchy.

items: Read four context cards (see model language).
For each, decide which syllabus emphasis would suit best and why.
Compare with a colleague.
Apply the same reasoning to your own context.
Write one change you could make within your constraints.
Add a card for your own school.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: A: Grade 10, state board exam in six months. → Skills-based with a structural backbone matched to the exam.
B: Adult hotel staff needing spoken English for guests. → Functional and task-based.
C: Grade 3, first year of English as R2. → Topic- and lexis-based, oral first, with songs and stories.
D: University first-years needing to read textbooks in English. → Skills-based (reading) with lexical focus on academic vocabulary.

body: Figure 12.8 A decision tree for syllabus emphasis

Purpose: to guide choice. Content: a simple decision tree starting with ‘Main need?’. Branches: ‘Exam’ → ‘Skills + structure’; ‘Spoken interaction at work’ → ‘Functions + tasks’; ‘Young beginners’ → ‘Topics + lexis, oral first’; ‘Academic reading’ → ‘Skills + academic vocabulary’. Style: clean flowchart. Board version: as described.

items: Excalidraw or draw.io (both free). Draw your own decision tree for your department.

body: Show your learners the contents page of their textbook and ask what they think the book is trying to teach them. Their answer shows what the syllabus communicates, which may be different from what its authors intended.

dek: Unit 12 of 100: structural, functional, lexical, task-based and skills-based syllabuses each organise a course around a different logic — knowing all five sharpens every planning decision.

aims.x: This unit sets out the main ways a language syllabus can be organized, and what each one makes easy or difficult. Its purpose is practical: to help teachers recognize the logic behind the syllabus they already use and make deliberate choices about it.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: describe structural, functional-notional, lexical, task-based and skills-based syllabuses;
identify which types a coursebook or state syllabus combines;
distinguish syllabus from curriculum and scheme of work;
choose a syllabus emphasis to suit a given context.

why: Why this matters. Most real courses blend syllabus types without naming them. Naming them lets a teacher choose deliberately instead of inheriting a coursebook's hidden logic.

background.x: A syllabus is a decision about what to teach and in what order. Every language course has one, even if no one wrote it down. The decision matters because language cannot be taught all at once, and the principle used to divide it up shapes almost everything that follows: what the textbook contains, what the tests measure and what learners come to believe language is.

Historically, the grammar of the language was the organizing principle. The communicative movement of the 1970s challenged this. David Wilkins’s Notional Syllabuses (1976) proposed organizing courses around meanings and functions instead. The COBUILD project at Birmingham led Dave Willis (1990) to propose a lexical syllabus based on the most frequent words and their patterns. Task-based approaches, developed by researchers including Michael Long and Graham Crookes (1992) and Rod Ellis (2003), proposed organizing courses around what learners do with language.

India has its own important place in this history. In the late 1970s and 1980s, N. S. Prabhu led the Communicational Teaching Project, often called the Bangalore Project, in which school classes in South India were taught through problem-solving tasks rather than a grammatical syllabus (Prabhu 1987). It is widely cited as one of the earliest large-scale experiments in task-based teaching anywhere.
Most real courses today mix several logics. The aim of this unit is not to pick a winner but to see the options clearly, so that choices about emphasis are made on purpose.

items: Syllabus analysis. Teachers produce a one-page analysis of their textbook’s syllabus blend and a supplementation plan.
Function repertoire. Learners show two ways to express each of five functions, with a note on politeness.
Task outcomes. In a task-based week, assess each task outcome (the survey, the poster) rather than a grammar test.
Pattern knowledge. Learners write sentences using four patterns of a frequent word.
What is the organizing principle of your textbook? Did you choose it, or was it chosen for you?
Which syllabus type is closest to how you would like to teach? What prevents you?
What do your learners believe learning English is ‘about’? Where does that belief come from?
How could you add a functional or task-based element to a structural syllabus without changing the book?
What can the Bangalore Project teach teachers working in large classes today?

terms.def: Prabhu’s project in South India (1979–84), in which school classes learned English through problem-solving tasks rather than a grammatical syllabus; one of the earliest large-scale trials of task-based teaching (Prabhu 1987).
The overall plan for education in a subject or institution, including its aims, content, methods and assessment; in India, national frameworks such as NCF 2023 guide state curricula.
The purpose a piece of language serves in communication, such as requesting, apologizing, advising or agreeing. A functional syllabus organizes teaching around such purposes (Wilkins 1976).
A syllabus organized around language functions, such as requesting or suggesting, and notions, such as time, quantity or location, rather than grammatical structures (Wilkins 1976).
A syllabus organized around the most frequent words, their meanings and the patterns they occur in, typically based on corpus evidence (Willis 1990).

A syllabus that combines several organizing strands, such as grammar, vocabulary, functions, skills and tasks, rather than following a single principle; most coursebooks and state syllabuses are of this kind.
A general concept that language expresses, such as time, quantity, location or frequency; notional syllabuses organize teaching around such meanings rather than grammatical forms (Wilkins 1976).
A term’s or year’s teaching plan that turns a syllabus into a sequence of units, with time allocations, review weeks and assessment points. It sits between the syllabus and individual lesson plans.
A syllabus organized around language skills and sub-skills, such as skimming, note-taking or giving a presentation, rather than grammar points or topics.

A syllabus organized around grammatical structures, sequenced roughly from simpler to more complex, such as the present simple before the present perfect. It was long dominant in Indian English textbooks.

A specification of what is to be taught in a course and, often, in what order, such as grammar points, functions, skills, topics or tasks. It is narrower than a curriculum and broader than a scheme of work.
A syllabus organized around a sequence of tasks rather than grammar points or topics, with language arising from task performance. Tasks are graded by complexity and familiarity.
